description: The workspace webview shows the ship-served lattice client, always through the loopback bridge (nav_decision in commands.rs allows no other http origin in that window), so the patterns are the bridge's sixteen ports only (proxy.rs, 26500 to 26515). Not http://127.0.0.1:* as it was: the shipless reader (reader.rs) is on 127.0.0.1 too, at 26520 to 26535, and its pages and the publishers' sandboxed frames inside them must get no command at all. It used to be any host, which granted these commands to any page the window might ever reach (security audit run-1). Everything here is still reachable by whatever the ship serves at the bridge origin, and each grant is justified on that basis. pick_upload, save_vault and pick_vault all open a native dialog and act ONLY on what the user then picks: a hostile page gets nothing without a visible OS dialog and a deliberate choice in it. open_external_url sends target=_blank links (the clearweb share link) to the system browser, refusing anything outside http, https, mailto and tel, enforced in rust rather than in the page. backup_write takes bytes for an EXISTING schedule id only; the page cannot choose the directory or the filename, both come from the stored schedule, and the schedule's own retention bounds how many files it can leave behind. NOTE: save_vault and pick_vault were missing here until the scheduled-backup work, which meant vault export and restore in the desktop app failed on 'not allowed. Command not found' — deny-by-default is right, but a command the client calls and never gets is a feature that silently does not exist. The queue-* commands back the offline queue and are called ONLY by the ship's own client, which is also the only thing that can produce an edit to queue. They read and write a per-ship directory under the app's data dir; a hostile page could fill that directory with junk it invented, which is bounded and visible, and is a far smaller risk than the alternative on the table — no offline queue at all, and edits lost every time the ship is unreachable. pandoc_probe and convert_tex were missing here for exactly the same reason save_vault and pick_vault were, and failed the same way: the button reported that pandoc was not installed on a machine where it was. Both are safe to grant. pandoc_probe runs `pandoc --version` and returns whether it worked, taking no argument from the page at all. convert_tex pipes the page’s own text through pandoc on stdin and returns the html, choosing the binary itself and never taking a path or a flag from the caller, so a hostile page can spend cpu converting its own text and nothing more. set_theme takes one boolean and sets the window's light/dark theme, so the GTK menubar and native scrollbars follow the page's colour scheme, and optionally the theme's CSS variables, kept so the manager page wears the same theme. Only theme.js's own variable names are kept, each only with a hex colour, light or dark, or a plain font list, so the worst a hostile page can do is pick the wrong colours. open_manager shows this app's own manager page (connection, mounts and scheduled backups), at its top or at one of its tabs (connection, files, backups); any other section name is refused. That is all it does: the manager page is a local origin the ship page cannot script, every command on it needs the user's own clicks there. A hostile page can call it to take the window off the ship page, skipping the editor's unsaved-work questions, which is a nuisance and can cost unsaved text, nothing more. take_urb_links hands the page the urb:// links other apps opened with lattice and empties the list. Every one was validated in rust as a plain urb://~ship/path before it was kept, and taking them is all the command does, so a hostile page can at worst swallow links the user asked to open. export_pdf writes a PDF of the html the page passes, and only to a file the user picks in a save dialog; the html is printed in a hidden window of its own with JavaScript off and no capability, so a hostile page gets a PDF of its own markup where the user chose to put one, nothing more. The This computer tabs of Settings (Connection, Files, Scheduled backups) now render in the ship page's own Settings tab, so it calls the shell's commands for them directly, and each is granted on the same basis. The reads, status, connection_status, reader_status, local_ships, list_mounts, backup_schedules and verify_backup, change nothing; the worst a hostile page learns is this computer's ship url and @p, the paths of its piers, mounts and backup folders, and whether its newest archive reads clean. pick_backup_dir opens a native folder dialog and returns only what the user picks there. Each command that changes something was checked for silent abuse. connect, add_mount, set_backup_schedules and clear_reader_history put the change to the user in a native dialog that names it (ship_page_asks in commands.rs, asked only when the caller is the bridge origin, never on the shell's own pages) and do nothing unless the user confirms: a hostile page cannot move this app onto its own ship, mount files into a folder of its choosing, add a schedule writing anywhere, pause or remove one, or empty the reading history unseen. run_backup_now writes one archive for an EXISTING schedule into that schedule's own folder, pruned by its own retention, so the harm is bounded to one extra archive. remove_mount unmounts a folder and forgets it; the files are the ship's and stay there, nothing is deleted, the user sees it in Files and can mount it again, so the harm is a visible, reversible nuisance. open_reader takes the window to the shipless reader, the same bounded nuisance as open_manager. export_reader_identity and import_reader_identity move the anonymous identity between computers (cometid.rs). export_reader_identity opens a native save dialog and writes the identity, sealed with the passphrase the caller passes, only to the file the user picks there; the page never gets the file's bytes, so a hostile page that knows the passphrase it passed still has no file unless the user saves one where it can read it, and the dialog's title says what is being saved. import_reader_identity opens a native open dialog and reads only the file the user picks, then always asks a native confirmation naming the identity being replaced and the one replacing it, and does nothing unless the user confirms; the replaced identity is moved aside in the app's data folder, never deleted. A hostile page can at worst show those dialogs unasked, a visible nuisance. The commands for a ship missing its software (stack_status, install_grubbery) stay off this list: a ship page that is running is a ship that has it, and install_grubbery would install a desk from a ship the caller names. open_manager stays granted for a ship UI older than this change, whose This computer tabs still go to the manager page. notify_share shows a system notification for a new share. It takes a title and a body, drops control characters and clips them to 120 and 200 characters in rust, and takes nothing else, so a hostile page can at worst show a short notification of its own words.
